In some parts of the world, vaccination can seem like a secondary concern as parents grapple with other tough issues. As one mother told Angu Glory, Cameroon Baptist Convention Health Services (CBCHS) Project District Officer: “There is no need for the vaccine because hunger will kill my child before any vaccine-preventable disease does.”  That comment reflects the harsh reality caregivers in this region face. “Families aren’t rejecting vaccines. They’re frustrated and overwhelmed by the daily struggles to survive,” Glory said.    Recognizing this issue, health workers in the area sought to improve vaccine uptake while helping families meet those additional needs.   The impact was immediate. More than 160,000 children were vaccinated, more than 68,000 were screened for malnutrition, over 1,000 received mosquito nets, and more than 13,000 caregivers received practical education on nutrition and vaccines. Through the Malaria Vaccine Learning Agenda, Sabin and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance brought together four research consortia that represented seven research projects across seven African countries, looking at malaria vaccine uptake. The preliminary findings point to practical solutions: stronger follow-up, better integration with routine child health services, earlier identification of missed children, and greater support for community health workers.   Why this matters: Malaria vaccine uptake falls significantly between the third and fourth doses. Finding solutions that work will ensure greater protection from one of the world’s largest health threats.  Read more in our latest newsletter, and subscribe for future updates. ⤵️ https://ow.ly/rBYx50Zwiga
